title: Windows Event Log Analysis and Sysmon Monitoring
description: Students install Sysmon on a Windows VM, simulate attacker behaviours (recon, persistence, lateral movement indicators), then investigate the resulting Event Log and Sysmon events using Event Viewer and PowerShell — building real incident detection skills.
objective: Students will configure enhanced Windows event logging with Sysmon, generate suspicious activity that mirrors common attacker techniques, then locate and interpret the resulting log entries — demonstrating the ability to detect attacker behaviours from Windows event data.

steps.title: Configure Enhanced Logging with Sysmon
steps.instructions:
Sysmon dramatically increases Windows logging visibility beyond the default Event Log.

**Download Sysmon:**
- Go to https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/sysinternals/downloads/sysmon
- Download Sysmon.zip and extract to C:\Tools\Sysmon\

**Download a quality config file:**
Open PowerShell as Administrator and run:
```powershell
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri 'https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SwiftOnSecurity/sysmon-config/master/sysmonconfig-export.xml' `
  -OutFile 'C:\Tools\Sysmon\sysmonconfig.xml'
```

**Install Sysmon with the config:**
```powershell
cd C:\Tools\Sysmon
.\Sysmon64.exe -accepteula -i sysmonconfig.xml
```

**Verify it's running:**
```powershell
Get-Service -Name Sysmon64
# Should show: Running
```

Sysmon events appear in: Event Viewer → Applications and Services Logs → Microsoft → Windows → Sysmon → Operational

Also enable command-line auditing for standard Event ID 4688:
```powershell
auditpol /set /subcategory:"Process Creation" /success:enable /failure:enable
```

steps.title: Simulate Attacker Recon Activities
steps.instructions:
Run commands that mimic what an attacker does after first getting into a Windows machine (post-exploitation recon).

**Open PowerShell as your normal user (not Administrator) and run:**
```powershell
# Attacker recon: who am I?
whoami
whoami /priv
whoami /groups

# What users are on this machine?
net user
Get-LocalUser

# Who is an administrator?
net localgroup administrators
Get-LocalGroupMember -Group 'Administrators'

# What processes are running?
Get-Process | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 10
tasklist /v

# What services are running?
Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq 'Running'} | Select-Object Name, DisplayName

# Network connections and listening ports
netstat -ano
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen
```

**Now open a new PowerShell window as Administrator and run:**
```powershell
# Check for credential stores
dir $env:APPDATA\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\
# (Shows PowerShell command history — attackers look here for passwords)

# Check scheduled tasks
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object {$_.State -eq 'Ready'}
```

Each of these commands generates Event ID 4688 (process create) entries. Continue to the next step.

steps.title: Simulate Persistence Mechanisms
steps.instructions:
Create the types of persistence mechanisms that attackers commonly use, then detect them.

**Persistence Method 1 — Registry Run Key:**
```powershell
# As your normal user:
$regPath = 'HKCU:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run'
Set-ItemProperty -Path $regPath -Name 'LabTest' -Value 'C:\Windows\Temp\backdoor.bat'
# Verify it was written:
Get-ItemProperty $regPath | Select-Object LabTest
```

**Persistence Method 2 — Scheduled Task:**
```powershell
# Create a scheduled task that runs at logon
$action = New-ScheduledTaskAction -Execute 'powershell.exe' -Argument '-WindowStyle Hidden -Command "Start-Sleep 5"'
$trigger = New-ScheduledTaskTrigger -AtLogOn
Register-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'WindowsUpdaterService' -Action $action -Trigger $trigger -RunLevel Highest
# List all scheduled tasks:
Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object {$_.TaskName -eq 'WindowsUpdaterService'}
```

**CLEAN UP — Remove the test persistence (important!):**
```powershell
Remove-ItemProperty -Path $regPath -Name 'LabTest'
Unregister-ScheduledTask -TaskName 'WindowsUpdaterService' -Confirm:$false
```

**Now detect these in the logs:**
```powershell
# Find Event ID 4698 (scheduled task created)
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4698} -MaxEvents 5 | Format-List
# Find Sysmon Event 13 (registry value set)
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational'; Id=13} -MaxEvents 10 |
  Where-Object {$_.Message -like '*CurrentVersion\Run*'} | Format-List
```

steps.title: Investigate Log Events with PowerShell
steps.instructions:
Now be the defender — investigate what the 'attacker' (you) did.

**Find all PowerShell process creation events from the last hour:**
```powershell
$startTime = (Get-Date).AddHours(-1)
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4688; StartTime=$startTime} |
  Where-Object {$_.Message -like '*powershell*'} |
  Select-Object TimeCreated, @{Name='Message';Expression={$_.Message.Substring(0,300)}} |
  Format-Table -AutoSize
```

**Find failed logon attempts (check for brute force):**
```powershell
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; Id=4625} -MaxEvents 20 | Format-List TimeCreated, Message
```

**Use Sysmon to trace process activity:**
```powershell
# Sysmon Event ID 1 = Process Created (includes full command line and parent)
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
  LogName='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational'
  Id=1
  StartTime=(Get-Date).AddMinutes(-30)
} | Select-Object TimeCreated, @{Name='Msg';Expression={$_.Message.Substring(0,400)}} | Format-List
```

**Check what connected to the network (Sysmon Event 3):**
```powershell
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{
  LogName='Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational'
  Id=3
} -MaxEvents 10 | Format-List
```

Document your findings. For each event, record: timestamp, event ID, process name, parent process, user account, and any command-line arguments visible.

steps.title: Write an Incident Investigation Report
steps.instructions:
Based on your simulated attack and the logs you collected, write a structured incident investigation report. This mirrors real Blue Team analyst work.

**Your report must include (in your PDF submission):**

**Executive Summary** (3–5 sentences)
Describe what activity was detected and what it suggests about attacker intent.

**Timeline of Events** (table format)
| Timestamp | Event ID | Source | Activity Detected |
|-----------|---------|--------|------------------|
| ... | 4688 | Security | powershell.exe created by ... |
| ... | 4698 | Security | Scheduled task 'WindowsUpdaterService' created |
| ... | Sysmon 1 | Sysmon/Operational | Process: net.exe, Parent: powershell.exe |

**Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)**
List any suspicious process names, registry keys, scheduled task names, or command-line arguments.

**Recommendations**
Write 3–5 specific actions a Windows administrator should take to prevent or detect this activity:
- Example: Enable PowerShell ScriptBlock logging (EventID 4104)
- Example: Deploy AppLocker to restrict execution from %TEMP%

**Screenshots required:**
- Sysmon running in services
- At least 3 event log entries from your investigation (Event Viewer or PowerShell output)
- The cleaned-up scheduled tasks list showing the test task has been removed

expected_output: Students submit: (1) PDF report with all 5 sections: Executive Summary, Event Timeline, IOCs, Recommendations, and screenshots. (2) At least 3 annotated event log screenshots showing Event IDs 4688, 4698, and at least one Sysmon event. (3) Written timeline documenting all suspicious activities they simulated and detected.
